en: The Sūtra for the Accomplishment of Vajrasattva (Vajrasattvasādhana).
Homage to Vajrasattva!

Those belonging to the lineage of the realization of the Buddha Vehicle, who are learned in the scriptures, having encountered a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), ascend to the Vajra Vehicle. Having entered into the meditative absorption (samādhi) of the yoga of the conceptual deity and turned away from the sixfold commentary, they propitiate a Vajrācārya.

Having heard the *Śrī Guhyasamāja Mahāyogatantra* by means of the literal meaning of the words, they extract [the essence] from the tantra for the sake of awakening the ignorant. Following the instructions as they have received them, they also compose the auxiliary practices (*sādhanāṅga*) of the yoga of the conceptual deity through various specific arrangements of terminology.
In that regard, some Vajrācāryas conceive of the accomplishment of Vajrasattva through the sequence of the moon and vajra;
some through the sequence of the arising of existence;
and some through the sequence of the fivefold manifest enlightenment.
Some conceive the accomplishment of Vajrasattva through the instantaneous method (*jhaṭiti-krama*).
Regarding the deities of the maṇḍala, some maintain that there are thirteen;
some, nineteen;
and some maintain the placement of twenty-five deities.
Thus, in this tantra, they bring forth the forms of deities such as Vajrasattva by relying on various causes;
accordingly, having composed commentaries (*ṭīkā*) and word-for-word glosses (*pañjikā*), they teach them to those beings to be trained.

(3) Therein, those who have faith in the Vajrayāna, having obtained their respective traditions by following their conviction, practice the yoga of the imagined deity through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and meditation.

Having understood this essential meaning, and having heard the Tantra through the gateway of the commentary on the six parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) according to the *Samāja-vyākhyā-tantra* transmitted by me from the lineage of the venerable Nāgārjuna, and having realized the two stages (*krama*),

I have composed this *melāpaka* (synoptic compendium) by sequentially extracting the sūtras concerning the accomplishment of Vajrasattva— both in his unified and differentiated forms— from up to the seventeenth chapter, for the sake of removing all doubt regarding the practice of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) for those who are intent upon its various modes.
In this regard, the sequence for hearing the means of accomplishment is first demonstrated: first is the memorization of the mantra; second is the instruction on ritual placement (nyāsa);
third is the systematic arrangement; and fourth is the vision of reality (tattvadarśana).
Having heard this sequence of means for accomplishment and having obtained the command of the Vajra Guru, one should offer an oblation before one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).

Then, the practitioner, in a place favorable to the mind such as a great forest, sitting facing east in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, should generate a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings and, for the sake of the welfare of oneself and others, accomplish the state of Vajrasattva according to the sequence to be described.
The sūtra for this is in the twelfth chapter: "In great forest regions adorned with fruits, flowers, and the like, or on a solitary mountain, one should accomplish the collection of all siddhis."
Thus [it is said].

Immediately thereafter, the practitioner, having removed ordinary ego-grasping through the resolve upon emptiness (*śūnyatādhimokṣa*), should instantly visualize himself in the form of Mahāvajradhara, white in color.

The scriptural authority for this is in the third chapter: "One should meditate on the Buddha-maṇḍala situated in the center of the space-element, a magnificent array of clouds of light rays, with a radiance equal to the blazing of a Buddha."
Thus [it is said].

Then, according to the method of the *Vajra-jñānapradīpa-samādhi* taught in the first chapter, one should recite the mantra *vajradhṛk*. Having visualized before oneself [the deity] in the form of Akṣobhya— black in color, with three faces and six arms—
one should then cause him to enter into one's own body by way of the "milk-and-water" analogy, and meditate upon oneself as being the color of sapphire in the form of Dveṣavajra.

The sūtra for this is in the first chapter: "The Vidyā-puruṣa of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, through the supreme state of union with the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Akṣobhya, in the form of black, white, and red, caused [him] to sit upon the vajra of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, within the vajra of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas."

Thus, the mantra-practitioner, established in the *dveṣavajra-samādhi*, should utter the long *hūṃ* syllable and visualize the ten wrathful deities, such as Yamāntaka, born from it—each with three faces and six arms, their hands busy with various weapons, stationed in the ten directions, and intent on threatening the wicked. The sūtra for this is in the thirteenth chapter: "The wrathful ones, born in the abode of hatred, are eternally intent upon slaying."
They are accomplished for the purpose of slaying by the practitioner who possesses the supreme dharma.
Thus [it is said].

Then, having emanated a second Nisumbharāja at the lower position from [the first] Nisumbharāja, and having visualized him standing before oneself in the form of a servant (*kiṅkara*) seeking an order, one should give the command with the four *hūṃ* mantras as stated in the fourteenth chapter:
In this regard, the mantra is: *oṃ sumbha nisumbha hūṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ ānaya ho bhagavan vidyārāja hūṃ phaṭ*.

Then, one should visualize Nisumbharāja going to the ten directions, drawing in the lords of the obstacles of the gods and others with a hook, binding them by the throat with a noose, and bringing them before the ten wrathful deities.

Then, having stationed Amṛtakuṇḍalin as a second emanation at the northern gate, one should emanate oneself in the form of the ten *kīla* (stake) deities and visualize them falling upon the heads of the ten lords of obstacles.
Then, one should meditate on Nisumbharāja rising up and striking [the stakes] while reciting the mantra with a vajra-hammer.

In this regard, the mantra is as follows: Oṃ gha gha gha gha ghātaya ghātaya all evil ones phaṭ phaṭ! Kīlaya kīlaya all sins phaṭ phaṭ! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! Vajrakīla, the Holder of the Vajra commands all obstructors’ bodies—(7)

Pierce the vajra of speech and mind, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Regarding this, the thirteenth chapter states: "One should visualize the great wrathful Vajrāmṛta as the Vajrakīla, blazing with a brilliant radiance of sparks; one should then drive it into the ten directions."
Thus [it is said].
Then, with the *ṭakkirāja* mantra, one should visualize four enclosures of iron, water, fire, and wind respectively on the outside.

This is the mantra: *ṭakki hūṃ jaḥ*. Then, with the syllable *bhrūṃ*, one should visualize a vajra-cage above, situated like a stūpa atop the iron enclosure; and with the three syllables, an armor; and with the syllable *hūṃ*, the ground consisting of a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*). One should contemplate these.
In this way, one should meditate upon the protection wheel preceded by the ritual procedures for binding the directions with boundaries, the vajra-fence, the vajra-canopy, and so forth.
Regarding its benefits, the thirteenth chapter states:
"The undertaking born of meditation is that which one should practice in whatever place."
Abiding by means of this yoga of meditation, one is empowered by the Buddhas.
Thus [it is said].
Then, with the verse on the awakening mind (bodhicitta) spoken in the second chapter, one should cause the protection wheel and the triple world to enter into suchness (*tathatā*).
In this regard, the verse is as follows: "In non-existence, there is no cultivation; cultivation is not at all cultivation.
Thus, existence would not be existence; cultivation is not perceived."
Thus it is said;
this too is the supreme protection.

Then, in the midst of the space-element, one should visualize a bow-shaped wind mandala from the syllable *yaṃ*, marked on its two sides by two *hūṃ* syllables and two vajras; above that, a triangular fire mandala from the syllable *raṃ*, marked by two vajras; again above that, a circular water mandala from the syllable *vaṃ*, marked by two vajras; and above that, a square earth mandala from the syllable *laṃ*, marked by two vajras. Having thus visualized these four mandalas, one should dissolve them and meditate upon the earth mandala alone.

Regarding this, the eleventh chapter of the Sūtra states: "One should visualize the maṇḍala born of all vajras situated in the center of the space-vajra. Therein, one should meditate upon the syllable *Bhrūṃ*, which brings forth clouds of vajras."
Thus [it is said].
Having thus produced the foundational maṇḍala, [one should visualize] a peaked pavilion by means of the syllable *bhrūṃ*, which is square, with four doors,
adorned with four archways, provided with four lines, and beautified by eight pillars.
Adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, and featuring gems, vajras, and crescent moons,
it is inlaid with vajra-jewels at the joints of the doors and projections.
The great vajra with a pot-shaped base and a pinnacle at the top,
adorned with bells and banners, and decorated with chowries and other ornaments.
Thus,
its sūtra is stated in the eighth chapter: (10) "A thousand yojanas in extent, square, and very beautiful."
And a shrine made of the four jewels, transparent and pure by nature.
Thus [it is said].

Having thus visualized an excellent palace, distinguished by such qualities and transcending those of gods and humans, situated upon the surface of the earth-mandala; having established the seat of the moon, sun, and so forth, and having personally cast off ordinary ego-grasping, one should instantly visualize oneself as the form of Mahāvajradhara—sapphire-colored, with three faces and six arms, holding a vajra, a wheel, and a lotus in the right hands, and a bell, a wish-fulfilling jewel, and a sword in the left hands, joined in the *sampuṭa* mudrā;
seated in the central mandala upon a lotus and moon seat in the sattva-paryaṅka posture.

Then, having visualized Vairocana in the east, Ratnasambhava in the south, Amitābha in the west, Amoghasiddhi in the north, Locanā in the southeast, Māmakī in the southwest, Pāṇḍaravāsinī in the northwest, and Tārā in the northeast within the inner maṇḍala; and [having visualized] Rūpavajrā in the southeast of the second enclosure, Śabdavajrā in the southwest, Gandhavajrā in the northwest, Rasavajrā in the northeast, and Sparśavajrā in the center— (11)
One should visualize her standing while embracing the Great Being (Mahāsattva).

Likewise, in the third enclosure, on the eastern frieze, one should visualize Maitreya and Kṣitigarbha; on the southern frieze, Vajrapāṇi and Khagarbha; on the western frieze, Lokeśvara and Mañjughoṣa; and on the northern frieze, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin and Samantabhadra. At the eastern gate, Yamāntaka; at the southern gate, Aparājita; at the western gate, Hayagrīva; and at the northern gate, Amṛtakuṇḍalin.
One should meditate on Acala in the southeast, Ṭakkirāja in the southwest, Nīladaṇḍa in the northwest, Mahābala in the northeast, Uṣṇīṣacakravartin above, and Niṣumbharāja below.
Regarding this, the Sūtra states in the first chapter: "It is transparent and of that very nature, yet possessing various forms on all sides;
it is filled with clouds of Buddhas and agitated by a dense mass of sparks."
The city of all the Tathāgatas is endowed with mandalas such as the Svaccha.
Thus [it is said].

Having thus resolved upon the manifestation of the thirty-two deities in the external maṇḍala, one should further arrange them within one’s own body-maṇḍala: the five Buddhas by way of the nature of the aggregates (*skandha*); the knowledge-deities (*vidyādevatā*) such as Rūpavajrā and others by way of the nature of the elements (*dhātu*); the Bodhisattvas by way of the nature of the sense-bases (*āyatana*); and the Wrathful Kings by way of the nature of the limbs.
The sūtra for this is in the seventeenth chapter: "In brief, the five aggregates are proclaimed as the five Buddhas;
the vajra-sense bases themselves are the maṇḍala of the supreme Bodhisattvas."
Earth is called Locanā, and the water element is remembered as Māmakī;
fire is called Pāṇḍarā, and wind is proclaimed to be Tārā.
The practitioner of mantras should always visualize the deity through forms, sounds, and so forth.
Thus, having understood this significance, the Blessed One stated in the *Sarvabuddhasamāyogaḍākinījālasaṃvara-mahāyogatantra*:
"Regarding the focus on a deity for those practitioners whose disposition is not directed toward reality (*atattva*)."
Yoga consisting of reflected images arises in [works such as] those that are cast and so forth.
What is the use of a deity as a focal point for those who possess the yoga of the disposition toward the true reality?
Through the yoga of the self and one's own samaya, the supreme unchanging is accomplished.
The self indeed is all-buddhahood and all-heroism;
therefore, with every effort, one should always worship the self.
Thus [it is said].

Thus, having caused the outer maṇḍala to enter into the body-maṇḍala, one should resolve that one’s own body-maṇḍala is composed of the atoms of all the Tathāgatas. Then, having sequentially dissolved the deities of the body-maṇḍala—who are of the nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—into the ultimate maṇḍala, one should solidify the *dharmakāya* with the mantra taught in the third chapter: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.
The scriptural authority for this is in the seventh chapter: (14)
If the semen should flow due to passion, one should drink it according to the prescribed rite out of a desire for the fruit;
thus one slays the array of Tathāgatas and will most certainly attain accomplishment.
Thus, having washed away all the stains of the afflictions by means of the object of emptiness, one should manifest oneself in the form of Vajrasattva Mahāmudrā through this sequence.

This is the sequence: from ultimate truth arises a sun mandala; above that, a moon mandala; again, above that, a red eight-petaled lotus; and upon the lotus, the three syllables Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ, stacked one above the other.

Having performed the placement [of the deities] and withdrawn everything, one should meditate on mind-only (cittamātra) transformed into the shape of a full moon disc. Having internalized within that the entire world of moving and non-moving beings, one should stabilize the jewel of one’s own mind with the mantra taught in the third chapter: *oṃ dharmadhātusvabhāvātmako ’ham*.
This is the first yoga.
Illuminating this point, he says in the *Saṃvara*: "The meditative attainment of mere gnosis is designated as 'yoga'."
Thus [it is said].
Then, above the lunar disc, one should meditate on the three syllables; from those, a vajra; and from the vajra, oneself in the form of Mahāvajradhara, white in color.
Vajrasattva, the great king, possesses a radiance equal to that of Vairocana.
Thus, from the statement in the fifteenth chapter:
this is the second inquiry.

Regarding this, the eleventh chapter of the Sūtra states: "The visualization of the Mahāmudrā should be performed by means of the supreme mantras of the three vajra-syllables, through the wisdom-vajra, which brings about the realization of all enlightenment."
Thus [it is said].

Having thus accomplished oneself as the saṃbhogakāya through the sequence of yoga and its application, one should, for the sake of sentient beings—like one in their final existence—produce oneself as the nirmāṇakāya by entering into the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases according to this sequence.
This is the sequence: having placed the syllable Oṃ, white in color and of the nature of Vairocana, upon the head, one should cause it to enter the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
Having thus placed the syllable ĀḤ, red in color and identical with Amitābha, upon the mouth, one should cause the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) to enter.
Having placed the syllable HŪṂ, black in color and identical with Akṣobhya, at the heart, one should cause the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) to enter.
Having placed the syllable SVĀ, yellow in color and identical with Ratnasambhava, at the navel, one should cause the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) to enter.
Having placed the green-colored syllable HĀKĀRA, whose nature is Amoghasiddhi, upon the two feet, one should cause it to enter the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).

Having placed Locanā as "delight in delusion" through the nature of the earth element, Māmakī as "delight in hatred" through the nature of the water element, Pāṇḍarā as "delight in passion" through the nature of the fire element, and Tārā as "delight in the vajra" through the nature of the wind element, one should conceive of [the elements] as hardness, fluidity, heat, and motion.

Having assigned Kṣitigarbha with the nature of the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*), Vajrapāṇi with the form of the ear-base (*śrotrāyatana*), Ākāśagarbha with the form of the nose-base (*ghrāṇāyatana*), Lokeśvara with the nature of the tongue-base (*jihvāyatana*), Mañjuśrī with the nature of the mind-base (*manaāyatana*), and Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin with the nature of the body-base (*kāyāyatana*), one should then visualize the divine eyes and so forth.
One should assign Maitreya, whose seed-syllable is *maiṃ*, with the nature of the sinews (*snāyu*).
One should place Samantabhadra together with his seed-syllable by means of the essential nature of the joints of the entire body.

Thus, having filled the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases through the empowerment by mantra, one should assign the ten wrathful deities (*krodha*)—emanating from long *hūṃ* syllables—to the limbs and members, such as the arms, in this sequence: Yamāntaka on the right arm, Aparājita on the left arm, Hayagrīva in the mouth, Amṛtakundalin in the secret place, Acala on the right upper arm, Ṭakkirāja on the left upper arm, Nīladaṇḍa on the right knee, Mahābala on the left knee, Uṣṇīṣacakravartin on the head, and Niṣumbharāja on the feet; having thus assigned them, one should cause them to enter the ten directions.

The sūtra for this is in the first chapter: "He empowered the form of the Great Knowledge-Man (mahāvidyāpuruṣa), which is the empowerment of the mantras of all Tathāgatas. Immediately upon being empowered, that very Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bodhicittavajra, appeared to all the Tathāgatas in a three-faced form. This is the third, the Atiyoga.

In this way, the practitioner, having removed his own natural ego-grasping (*prākṛtāhaṅkāra*) through the three yogas and having accomplished the form of Śrī Vajrasattva, should perform the fourth, the Mahāyoga, in order to eliminate the conceptualizations of both the deity being formed and the deity already accomplished.

Therein, having visualized a white syllable *Oṃ* at the crown of the head, one should contemplate a multitude of Locanās produced from it within the hollow of space by means of the application of sovereign power.
Then, having suddenly beheld the array of Vairocana in the intermediate space through the application of mastery, one should supplicate him with the two verses stated in the twelfth chapter:
In this regard, the verse is as follows: The glorious bearer of the Buddha-body, cultivated through the indivisibility of the three vajras.
May the Holder of the Body-Vajra bestow upon me today the state of empowerment.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are realized as the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra-Body holders!

Immediately following the request, having experienced the bliss of supreme joy preceded by mutual passion within the array of deities, one should visualize [the deity] entering through the door of Vairocana in the form of white light rays, like the Knowledge Being (*jñānasattva*), reaching the ground of gnosis, filling the entire body, and bringing it delight; then, one should stabilize this with the verse taught in the seventh chapter.
This is the verse: "That body of all the Buddhas, which is filled with the five aggregates..."
By virtue of the nature of the Buddha-body, may mine also become like that.

Thus, one should then generate the non-dual ego-sense with the mantra taught in the sixth chapter: *oṃ sarvatathāgatakāyavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* (I am of the nature of the vajra-body of all the Tathāgatas).
(19) One should also perform the consecration of speech and mind by this very same sequence.

The sequence therein is as follows: having placed the syllable *ĀḤ*, red in color, upon the lotus of the mouth, and having filled the sky with the emanations of Pāṇḍaravāsinī produced therefrom, one should behold the array of Amitābha as before and entreat him with this verse:
"The glorious Dharma is indeed the path of speech, cultivated through the indivisibility of the three vajras."
May the Vajra of Speech grant me the state of empowerment this very day.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are meditated upon as the indivisible three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra of Speech!

When thus entreated, as before, through the union of the two organs, the two arrays melt by the fire of great passion and enter one’s mouth in the form of red rays; having visualized this as bestowing the sovereignty of all speech, one should stabilize it with this verse: “Whatever perfection of expression belongs to the speech of Vajradharma, may my speech likewise become like that of the Holder of Dharma.”
(20) Thus, one should then generate the ego-sense of non-duality with this mantra.
In this regard, the mantra is: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the speech-vajra of all Tathāgatas*.

Then, having visualized a black-syllable *hūṃ* upon the central prong of a vajra within one’s own heart, and having visualized the resulting array of Māmakī filling the expanse of the sky, one should likewise instantly behold the array of Akṣobhya in the intermediate space and supplicate him with this verse: “O glorious holder of the vajra-mind, meditated upon as the indivisibility of the three vajras,
may you today grant me the state of empowerment of the Vajra-Mind.”
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are meditated upon as the indivisible three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra-Mind!

Immediately following the prayer, one should visualize that—as before—the two arrays melt into a state of great passion by means of the fire of great passion; entering the heart in the form of black rays, they bring about mastery over the mind.
One should then stabilize this with the following verse: “Whatever the mind of Samantabhadra, the wise Lord of Secrets, may my mind also become just like that, equal to the Vajra-holder.”
(21) Thus, he should then form the ego-identity of non-duality with this: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-mind of all Tathāgatas."

Thus, having entered the three families and having separately empowered body, speech, and mind, one should again perform the empowerment of Mahāvajradhara by means of the indivisible nature of the three vajras, according to this sequence: *oṃ sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* (I am of the nature of the vajra of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas).
The sūtra for this is in the second chapter: "May you generate the mind in the form of the body, the body in the form of the mind, and the mind through the utterance of speech."
Because he is accomplished by means of the method of the vajra-samādhi arising from the samaya as described in the first chapter, he is called the *samayasattva*.

Having thus generated the Samayasattva with three faces and six arms, one should visualize the Jñānasattva within his heart—two-armed and red in color—satisfying his entire body through the *sampuṭa* union;
then, one should meditate on the Lord upon one’s own crown.
Regarding this, the Sūtra states in the twelfth chapter: "Endowed with the excellence of all aspects, he is the Vajra of one's own body, speech, and mind."
In the heart is Jñānasamaya, and on the crown is Vajrāgradhārin.
(22) This is the supreme commitment that pleases all Buddhas;
it must be performed by one at the forefront of the commitment, for it is the highest bringer of all accomplishments.

Thus, having visualized the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) within the heart of the commitment-being (*samayasattva*), one should meditate upon the syllable *HŪṂ*—known as the concentration-being (*samādhisattva*)—within the heart of that wisdom-being as well. This [syllable] is ever-arising, resembling a great lamp, and has the form of a mass of light for the purpose of dispelling the darkness of ignorance. Regarding this, the sūtra states in the eleventh chapter: "One should visualize Vajrākṣobhya situated in the center of the Buddha-maṇḍala."
Having meditated on the syllable HŪṂ at the heart, one should place the mind within the drop (bindu).
Thus ends the Mahāyoga.

Thus, having accomplished the King of Samādhis— the supreme sovereign of meditative absorptions— which consists of the perfection of one’s own welfare and has as its nature the self composed of the three beings by means of the fourfold yoga, the introductory section is now introduced in order to demonstrate the King of Maṇḍalas, the supreme sovereign of meditative absorptions, for the sake of the perfection of the welfare of others.

The Blessed One Śākyamuni, having performed all [these deeds], descended from the sublime realm of Tuṣita, manifested a form free from passion, established those of the Śrāvaka lineage on the path of the Śrāvakas, and then [established] the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas...
Having elucidated the path of the perfections (pāramitāmārga),
this [teaching] is intended to demonstrate that enlightenment arises from passion for those who have faith in the profound.

In that regard, having entered the meditative absorption (samādhi) called the "Method of Great Passion" as described in the first chapter, the yogi practicing accordingly should likewise perform the initial yoga in order to demonstrate the liberation through desire to sentient beings whose conduct is dominated by passion.
One should dwell by means of the samādhi for the enjoyment of all desires as taught in the seventeenth chapter, following this sequence.

This is the sequence: having taken an external consort endowed with all auspicious marks and well-trained in mantra and tantra, and having placed her before oneself, one should form the union of the five families.

Then, preceded by the consecration of the vajra and lotus, having entered into the union of the two organs and emanated the maṇḍala-circle of Akṣobhya and the other deities from the *bodhicitta*, one should purify the afflictions of sentient beings, such as hatred and the rest, through their respective samādhis.
Having brought it back, one should cause it to enter one's own body-maṇḍala.
Alternatively, having emanated a wisdom-mudrā from one's own heart and entered into union with her, one should accomplish the welfare of sentient beings through the single emanation of the mantra.
The Great Goddess residing in the heart is the bearer of yoga for yogins.
She is known as Vajradhātvīśvarī, the mother of all Buddhas.

Thus it is stated in the *Sarvarahasyatantra*. Regarding this, the aphorism in the seventh chapter says: "Having obtained such a woman sixteen years of age, radiant with beauty, one should begin the worship in secret by means of the three stages of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*)."
One should visualize Locanā, the great consort of the Tathāgata;
through the union of the two organs, one shall attain the siddhi of a Buddha.
Thus it is said.
Having thus determined the external and internal mudrās, the sequence of the assembly of the five families is now demonstrated:
one should place Oṃ at the head, Āḥ at the mouth, Hūṃ at the heart, Svā at the navel, and Hā at the feet.
One should place Locanā and the others according to the nature of the four elements.
One should place the Vajra-forms and others by way of the intrinsic nature of objects such as form.
Furthermore, one should place the Wrathful Queens upon her limbs and other members:
therein, Vajravetālī on the right arm, Aparājitā on the left arm, and Bhṛkuṭī on the face. (25)

One should place Kuṭī in the secret place, Ekajaṭā on the right arm, Viśvavajrī on the left arm, Viśvaratnī on the right knee, Viśvapadmī on the left knee, Viśvakarmī on the head, Gaganavajriṇī on the feet, and Dharaṇīndharī [on the soles of the feet].

Regarding this, the sūtra states in the eighth chapter: "The knower of the ritual should place [the goddesses] from the space between the breasts up to the middle of the topknot, and also within the space between the feet."
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the five families upon the navel, the hips, and the secret place of the sons of the Victors.
Thus [it is said].
Having thus performed the ritual preparation and removed the ordinary female form, one should perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the vajra and lotus according to this sequence:
The consecration of the vajra is as follows: having visualized one's own *liṅga* as a five-pronged vajra by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should place the syllable *OṂ* upon the central prong.
The consecration of the lotus is as follows: having placed the syllable *ĀḤ* within her *dharmodaya*, one should meditate on the red eight-petaled lotus produced from it.
The sūtra for this is in the seventh chapter: "One should conceptualize the syllable HŪṂ, the syllable OṂ, and the syllable PHAṬ;
one should meditate upon a vajra and a lotus, pervaded by five-colored rays of light."
(26) Thus it is said.

Then, possessing the pride (*ahaṅkāra*) of Ratnasambhava, and having performed embracing, kissing, and so forth, preceded by mutual passion, one should generate the pride of non-duality with the mantra taught in the sixth chapter.

There, this is the mantra: *oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* ("I am of the nature of the vajra of the passion of all Tathāgatas"). This is the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Ratnasambhava. Then, uttering the song of the syllable *hūṃ*, one should become engaged in the activity of the woman.
In the state of emission, one should utter the *phaṭ* mantra.

Then, the deities of the maṇḍala of the body, having experienced the bliss of supreme joy (*paramānanda*), descend into the center of the lotus from the hollows of the channels in the form of drops (*bindu*).
The sūtra for this is in the first chapter: "He dwells within the bhagas of the vajra-ladies, who are the heart-vajras of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas."

Thus, having resolved upon the empowerment of Amoghasiddhi while in the state of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should cultivate the non-dual ego-sense with the offering mantra taught in the sixth chapter.
There, this is the mantra: *oṃ sarvatathāgatapūjāvajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* ("Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the worship of all Tathāgatas").

Thus, having empowered oneself through the entry into the five Tathāgatas, and having cultivated the ego-identity consisting of all families up to the conclusion of the meditative absorption, consecration, and worship, one should emanate the maṇḍala circle by way of the process of arising in existence for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others.
Therein, through the meditative absorption of Akṣobhya, one effects the purification of the affliction of hatred in sentient beings.
Thus, through the Vairocana-samādhi, there is the purification of delusion;
through the Ratnasambhava-samādhi, the purification of pride;
and through the Amitābha-samādhi, the purification of passion.
Through the samādhi of Amoghasiddhi, there is the purification of envy.
That same Blessed One brings peace to sentient beings through the samādhi of Locanā,
and nourishment through the samādhi of Māmakī.
Through the *pāṇḍaravāsinī-samādhi*, he provides protection;
through the *tārā-samādhi*, he effects subjugation (*vaśya*).
That very Blessed One, having become Rūpavajrā and the others, brings about happiness and mental well-being for sentient beings.
That very Blessed One effects the purification of the sense-bases of sentient beings through the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of bodhisattvas such as Kṣitigarbha.
That very Blessed One threatens the hosts of obstructors in the ten directions through the wrathful meditative absorptions of Yamāntaka and others.
For the Blessed One Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata, is indeed the union of all.
Indeed, its enjoyment is the entirety of the three realms without exception.
Thus it is said. This is the second samādhi, named Maṇḍalarājāgrī (The Supreme King of Mandalas).
Having thus manifested the wheel of the thirty-two deities and performed the subtle yoga and the external and internal recitation, one should again cause oneself to enter into suchness (*tathatā*).

Then, the four goddesses beginning with Locanā, not perceiving great bliss (*mahāsukha*) in the center of the mandala, awaken that great bliss through songs beginning with "O Vajracitta," out of the distress caused by their separation.
In this regard, there is this song: “O Vajra-Mind, Lord of the World, Refuge of the realm of beings, protect me with your delightful passion for the sake of the great purpose!
Love me, O Father, supreme kinsman of beings, if you desire my life, O Protector!”
O Vajra-body, whose embrace is dear to many beings, O Wheel of the Buddhas' purpose, who perceives the welfare and the ultimate meaning of enlightenment!
If you desire my life, O Protector, then love me with passion, according to the pledge of passion.
O Vajra Speech, you who are compassionate for the welfare of all and ever engaged in performing deeds for the sake of the world—
(29) O Samantabhadra, desire me in the practice of supreme bliss, if you wish for my life, O Lord!

O Vajrakāma, supreme of commitments, you who act for the great benefit of others, the ornament of the lineage of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, and compassionate through equanimity— desire me, a treasury of virtues and a source of many jewels, if you wish for my life, O Lord!

When he has been thus exhorted by his truly existent qualities, the Tathāgatas praise him as he emerges from meditative absorption through the power of his former vows, with these royal hymns of praise beginning with "Akṣobhya.
Therein, this is the praise: "O Akṣobhya-vajra, great wisdom, Vajradhātu, great enlightened one! O Triple Mandala, supreme among the three vajras, speak the secret; homage be to you!"
Vairocana, greatly pure, vajra-peaceful, great delight! Teach the phenomena that are luminous by nature; O Vajra, homage be to you!
O King of Jewels, most profound, stainless as the space of the vajra-sky, pure by nature and beyond destruction—speak the secret; homage be to you!
O Vajrāmita, Great King, free from conceptual construction, holder of the space-vajra;
you who have attained the perfection of passion, speak, O Vajra—homage be to you!
O Amoghavajra, perfectly awakened one, fulfiller of all hopes,
born of pure intrinsic nature, Vajrasattva, homage be to you!

Immediately thereafter, having revealed the Buddha-knowledge and having delighted the mandala-circle, one should perform the conclusion by entering it into one’s own body-mandala according to the previous procedure, following this sequence:

having uttered the syllable *HŪṂ* residing in one’s own heart, one should contemplate all the realms of sentient beings as transformed into the form of Mahāvajradhara, and dwell with that mental focus. The scriptural authority for this is found in the tenth chapter: "One should meditate upon the arrayed mandala situated in the center of the space-element."
(31) One should visualize the syllable *hūṃ* situated there in the center as one's own form.
Thus [it is said].

Thus, a beginner who has established the vows of the samaya, received initiation, abandoned ordinary egoism, and is eager to accomplish the welfare of self and others through the practice of yoga with the deities of the four junctions (*saṃdhyā*), should perform even the most distinguished rites such as pacification (*śāntika*).
Having purified the food, the throat, and the heart according to the sequence taught in the *Sādhana*, he should partake of his meal; thus it will be easily digested.

One should accomplish all activities through external and internal homa, by means of the three-syllable mantra or the garland-mantra, and also through the application of mantras and medicinal herbs, as well as the union of the lotus and the vajra.
This is the third samādhi, named the Supreme King of Activities.
In the *Śrī Guhyasamāja Mahāyoga Tantra*, the sūtra on the accomplishment of Vajrasattva through the stage of generation is complete.
This is the work of the venerable master Candrakīrti. (32)
